influences/mary-isis-debate/name: Mary, Isis and the mother-goddess debate
influences/mary-isis-debate/sourceCultur: Isis nursing the infant Horus (Isis lactans) and the titles and devotions of Isis and other mother goddesses
influences/mary-isis-debate/christianFor: Images of the Virgin and Child, especially the nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa), and Marian titles and devotion
influences/mary-isis-debate/evidenceNote: Some iconographic influence of Isis-and-Horus images on Egyptian and Byzantine images of the nursing Virgin is plausible and argued by respected art historians. That Marian doctrine or devotion originated in the Isis cult is not supported: it grew from the Gospels, the second-century Protevangelium of James and the fifth-century debates about Christ. Claims that Mary is simply Isis, Ishtar or Semiramis renamed belong to polemic, not historical evidence.
influences/mary-isis-debate/popularClaim: The Virgin Mary is the Egyptian goddess Isis (or the Babylonian ‘Queen of Heaven’) in Christian dress: the Madonna and Child were copied from Isis and Horus, and the church adopted a mother goddess to win pagans.
influences/mary-isis-debate/whatHistoria: Historians distinguish image from belief. Visually, the seated mother suckling a divine child was an established Egyptian type, and Thomas Mathews and Norman Muller have argued that painted Isis panels were among the models for early Marian icons; Coptic Galaktotrophousa images strengthen the case. But the mother-and-child pose is near-universal, and the earliest Christian example (Catacomb of Priscilla, third century) is not Egyptian. Marian devotion has clear Christian roots: the infancy narratives, the Protevangelium of James (c. 150), the Eve–Mary typology of Justin and Irenaeus, and the title Theotokos, defended by Cyril of Alexandria and proclaimed at Ephesus in 431 to safeguard the unity of Christ. Church leaders also explicitly opposed goddess-like worship of Mary, as Epiphanius did with the Collyridians. Scholars such as R. E. Witt argued for strong Isiac influence on popular piety, while Stephen Shoemaker, Hilda Graef and Jaroslav Pelikan locate the origins of Marian devotion within Christian tradition; the debate is real but concerns influence on forms of piety and art, not the source of the doctrine.
influences/mary-isis-debate/summary: Images of the Virgin nursing the Christ child resemble Egyptian images of Isis nursing Horus, and scholars debate the extent of artistic and devotional influence; the popular claim that Mary is a renamed Isis is not supported by evidence.
influences/mary-isis-debate/story:
Isis was one of the most popular deities of the Roman Empire. Her cult spread from Egypt across the Mediterranean, with temples in Rome, Pompeii and London; Apuleius’s Golden Ass (book 11, second century) gives a famous hymn to her as queen of heaven and mother of all. Egyptian art had for many centuries shown her seated, suckling the infant Horus, and her worshippers celebrated her as protector of seafarers (Isis Pelagia), healer and saviour. At Philae in Upper Egypt her temple remained active until c. 535–537, when Justinian’s general Narses closed it; part of it was later converted into a church of St Stephen.

The resemblance between Isis lactans and images of the Virgin nursing Christ has been noticed since the Enlightenment. The earliest Christian image of Mary and the child, in the Catacomb of Priscilla in Rome (early to mid-third century), shows a seated woman holding an infant beside a prophet pointing to a star. In Egypt the nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa or Maria lactans) appears in Coptic wall paintings at the monasteries of Apa Jeremias at Saqqara and Apa Apollo at Bawit (sixth to seventh centuries). Thomas Mathews and Norman Muller argued in 2005 that late-antique painted panels of Isis were a direct model for early Marian icons, a view many art historians find plausible for Egypt while noting that the mother-and-child pose is common to many cultures.

Marian belief, however, had its own Christian sources. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell of the virginal conception; Justin Martyr (c. 155) and Irenaeus (c. 180) developed Mary as the new Eve; the Protevangelium of James (c. 150) narrated her birth and perpetual virginity. The title Theotokos (‘God-bearer’) was used in Alexandria by the early fourth century, and the prayer Sub tuum praesidium, addressed to the Theotokos, survives on a papyrus variously dated between the third and seventh centuries. When Nestorius of Constantinople objected to the title in 428, warning against making the Virgin a goddess, Cyril of Alexandria defended it as a statement about Christ: the child Mary bore was God the Word incarnate. The Council of Ephesus (431) agreed with Cyril, and Marian devotion grew rapidly afterwards.

That the council met in Ephesus, the city of Artemis (Acts 19), has encouraged claims that the Theotokos replaced the Ephesian goddess, but the choice of venue and the outcome were driven by ecclesiastical politics and Christology. The church explicitly rejected goddess-like cult: Epiphanius of Salamis (Panarion 79, c. 377) condemned the Collyridians, women in Arabia who offered bread-cakes to Mary as a priestess would to a goddess, insisting that ‘Mary is to be honoured, but the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are to be worshipped’. Later titles once linked to Isis have other derivations: ‘Star of the Sea’ (Stella maris) arose from Jerome’s etymology of Miriam as ‘drop of the sea’ (stilla maris), and ‘Queen of Heaven’ (Regina caeli) developed from biblical imagery of the woman in Revelation 12 and Mary’s place in Christ’s kingdom; the ‘queen of heaven’ condemned in Jeremiah 7 and 44 was a Near Eastern goddess and was never identified with Mary by the church.

The modern debate has been sharpened by Protestant polemic. Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853) identified Mary with Semiramis and Isis as part of an attack on Roman Catholicism, and his claims still circulate though historians have long rejected his method. Scholars such as R. E. Witt (Isis in the Graeco-Roman World, 1971) argued for real Isiac influence on popular piety; others, including Stephen Shoemaker, Hilda Graef and Jaroslav Pelikan, emphasise the internal Christian development of Marian devotion. A fair summary is that late-antique Christians lived among images and devotions to divine mothers and may have borrowed artistic forms, while the content of Marian doctrine was shaped by debates about who Christ is.
influences/mary-isis-debate/howItHappene: Christian artists in Egypt and elsewhere drew on familiar images of seated mothers and divine infants, including Isis and Horus.
The Christological controversies of the fifth century made the title Theotokos a test of orthodoxy and stimulated Marian feasts, churches and images.
As pagan temples closed, some former devotees of Isis and other goddesses became Christians and may have carried habits of piety with them.
Bishops drew boundaries, distinguishing honour paid to Mary from worship due to God alone (later formalised as hyperdulia versus latria).
Protestant and Enlightenment polemicists from the seventeenth century onwards highlighted the parallels to attack Catholic devotion.
influences/mary-isis-debate/examples/0: Virgin and Child with a prophet, Catacomb of Priscilla, Rome (third century).
influences/mary-isis-debate/examples/1: Nursing Virgin (Galaktotrophousa) at the Monastery of Apa Jeremias, Saqqara (sixth–seventh century), now in the Coptic Museum, Cairo.
influences/mary-isis-debate/examples/2: Egyptian terracotta and bronze figurines of Isis lactans nursing Horus (Roman period).
influences/mary-isis-debate/examples/3: The Temple of Isis at Philae, closed c. 535–537 and partly converted to a church.
influences/mary-isis-debate/examples/4: Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome, rebuilt by Sixtus III (432–440) after the Council of Ephesus, with mosaics of Christ’s infancy.
influences/mary-isis-debate/defenders/0/: Defended the title Theotokos against Nestorius as a confession that Mary’s son is God incarnate, making Marian honour an expression of Christology.
influences/mary-isis-debate/defenders/1/: Wrote homilies on the Dormition and distinguished the honour given to the Theotokos and saints from the worship due to God alone.
influences/mary-isis-debate/critics/0/te: Condemned the Collyridians for offering cakes to Mary as a goddess: ‘Let Mary be honoured, but let the Lord be worshipped’ (Panarion 79).
influences/mary-isis-debate/critics/1/te: Objected to the title Theotokos in 428, warning that it risked making the Virgin a goddess; condemned at Ephesus in 431.
influences/mary-isis-debate/critics/2/te: His anti-Catholic The Two Babylons (1853) identified Mary with Isis and Semiramis; the book remains influential in some circles despite its discredited method.
influences/mary-isis-debate/keptBy/0: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, which honour Mary as Theotokos and reject the claim of pagan origin.
influences/mary-isis-debate/keptBy/1: Anglican and Lutheran traditions, which keep some Marian feasts and the title Theotokos as defined at Ephesus.
influences/mary-isis-debate/rejectedBy/0: Reformed and many evangelical Protestants, who reject Marian invocation and often see parallels with goddess cults as a warning.
influences/mary-isis-debate/rejectedBy/1: Jehovah’s Witnesses and some fundamentalist writers, whose literature has drawn on Hislop’s identification of Mary with pagan goddesses.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/nam: Amulets, charms, folk magic and the church
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/sou: Protective amulets, spoken charms, divination and healing magic, as in the Greek Magical Papyri and Germanic charms
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/chr: Christian amulets with Scripture and the cross, healing charms invoking saints, sortes biblicae, sacramentals and blessings
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/evi: Christian amulets and charms that adapt pagan formulae survive in large numbers, from Egyptian papyri to Anglo-Saxon manuscripts, and church leaders constantly condemned the practice, so the continuity of folk practice is beyond doubt. What is debated is how far the church deliberately accommodated magic (Valerie Flint’s thesis) and how far sacramentals and blessings themselves should be seen as ‘Christian magic’ (Keith Thomas) — a framing that itself reflects Protestant polemic.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/pop: Medieval Christianity was mostly pagan magic with Christian words, and holy water, medals and blessings are just charms.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/wha: Late antique Egypt has yielded many papyrus and parchment amulets with the Lord’s Prayer, Psalm 91, gospel incipits and the names of saints, sometimes mixed with older magical names and symbols; the Greek Magical Papyri show the pagan background. Bishops responded ambivalently: the Council of Laodicea (c. 363, canon 36) forbade clergy to make phylacteries; John Chrysostom attacked amulets but urged the sign of the cross instead; Augustine preferred that a sick person lay the Gospel on his head than run to an amulet (Tractates on John 7.12). In early medieval Europe Caesarius of Arles and councils such as Agde (506) condemned amulets and ‘lots of the saints’, while Anglo-Saxon charms such as the Æcerbot field remedy combined Masses and the Lord’s Prayer with invocations of ‘Erce, mother of earth’. Keith Thomas argued that the medieval church offered a kind of ‘church magic’ which Protestantism stripped away, while Eamon Duffy and others insist that late medieval devotion was coherent Christian piety, not paganism. Catholic theology distinguishes sacramentals, which work through the church’s prayer, from superstition, which it condemns.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/sum: Christians inherited a world in which amulets and charms were everywhere. The church condemned magic while offering Christian alternatives — the cross, Scripture, relics and blessings — and the boundary between devotion and magic was contested from late antiquity to the Reformation and beyond.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/sto:
In the Roman world almost everyone wore or used protection against illness, the evil eye and demons: inscribed gems, metal lamellae, knotted cords and papyrus slips with powerful names. The Greek Magical Papyri from Egypt preserve the recipes, often mixing Egyptian, Greek and Jewish divine names. Converts did not suddenly stop worrying about fever, childbirth or crops, and the New Testament itself records magicians becoming Christians and burning their books at Ephesus (Acts 19:19).

The church’s leaders were consistently hostile to magic but realistic about need. The Council of Laodicea (c. 363, canon 36) forbade clergy to be magicians, astrologers or makers of phylacteries. John Chrysostom condemned women who hung amulets, bells and red threads on children and mocked those who hung gospel books round their necks (Homilies on Matthew 72), yet recommended the sign of the cross as protection. Augustine told his congregation that he would praise a sick man who laid the Gospel on his head rather than go to an amulet, though he wished they would simply pray (Tractates on John 7.12). Surviving Christian amulets from Egypt, with the Lord’s Prayer, Psalm 91 or the opening of each gospel, show what ordinary believers actually did.

In the early medieval West the pattern continued. Caesarius of Arles (died 542) preached against diviners, ligatures and charms; the Council of Agde (506, canon 42) forbade the ‘lots of the saints’, consulting the Bible at random for guidance, a practice that nonetheless persisted. Anglo-Saxon manuscripts preserve charms such as the Æcerbot, in which a priest says Masses over sods of earth taken from a field while the farmer invokes ‘Erce, Erce, Erce, mother of earth’, and the Nine Herbs Charm, which names Woden alongside Christ. Valerie Flint argued that churchmen deliberately ‘rescued’ certain magical practices by Christianising them; Richard Kieckhefer and others see a more untidy coexistence of learned and popular culture.

The late Middle Ages had a rich system of blessed objects — holy water, Agnus Dei wax medallions, candles from Candlemas, palm crosses — and prayers to saints for protection against plague, fire and storms. Keith Thomas’s Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) argued that Protestants rejected much of this as ‘popish magic’ and so contributed to the decline of magical thinking, though cunning folk, charms and witch beliefs remained widespread among Protestants too, and the early modern witch-hunts were driven by learned demonology in both confessions. Eamon Duffy’s The Stripping of the Altars (1992) argues that such devotions were integral to a coherent Catholic faith rather than pagan survivals.

The debate continues in global Christianity. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2111–2117) condemns superstition, divination and wearing charms while commending sacramentals; Orthodox Christians wear crosses and use blessed oil and water; many Pentecostal and African Initiated Churches confront traditional charms directly, sometimes burning fetishes publicly while offering anointing oil, prayer cloths and blessed water — practices that critics in turn describe as new forms of Christian magic.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/how: Converts continued to seek protection against illness and evil spirits, using amulets and charms.
Christian formulae — the Lord’s Prayer, Psalm 91, gospel openings, the cross and saints’ names — replaced or joined pagan names on amulets.
Bishops and councils condemned magic while recommending the sign of the cross, prayer, Scripture and blessings instead.
Early medieval charms combined Christian liturgy with older invocations, especially for healing and fertility.
Protestant reformers attacked blessed objects as magic; Catholic theology distinguished sacramentals from superstition.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/exa: Christian papyrus amulets from Egypt with the Lord’s Prayer and Psalm 91 (fourth to seventh centuries)
Council of Laodicea (c. 363), canon 36, against clergy making phylacteries
Augustine, Tractates on John 7.12: the Gospel on the head rather than an amulet
Council of Agde (506), canon 42, condemning the ‘lots of the saints’
The Anglo-Saxon Æcerbot field charm invoking ‘Erce, mother of earth’ with Masses and the Lord’s Prayer
Agnus Dei wax medallions and Candlemas candles in late medieval devotion
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/def: Accepted the Gospel book laid on a sick person’s head as a lesser evil than pagan amulets, a model of accommodation.
Urged believers to protect children with the sign of the cross instead of amulets (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 12).
His Dialogues popularised the protective power of the cross, holy water and saints’ relics against demons.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/cri: Condemned amulets, incantations and gospel books worn as charms (Homilies on Matthew 72).
Preached repeatedly against amulets, diviners and charms among baptised Christians in sixth-century Gaul.
Treated holy water, blessed candles and similar objects as superstitious remnants of paganism and popery.
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/kep: Catholic Church (sacramentals: holy water, medals, blessings — distinguished from superstition)
Eastern Orthodox churches (blessed water, oil and crosses)
Folk Christianity across Europe, Latin America, Africa and Asia
Some Pentecostal and African Initiated Churches (anointing oil, prayer cloths, blessed water)
influences/amulets-charms-folk-magic/rej: Official Catholic and Orthodox teaching, which condemns charms and divination as superstition
